original_query: linearly extractable directions in the residual stream that encode social/demographic variables (gender, age, framing, meeting condition) in an LLM dictator-game decision agent; contrastive paired-prompt difference vectors; decorrelation for pure per-variable directions; activation-addition steering both signs; selectivity

sub_queries.hyde_text: We investigate whether large language models internally encode the influence of social and contextual variables — such as gender, age, instruction framing, and meeting condition — as low-dimensional linear directions in the residual stream when they act as economic decision agents. Using paired prompts that differ only in the target variable (male vs female, young vs old, framing A vs B, meeting vs no-meeting), we extract per-variable difference vectors from hidden activations and characterize how these directions relate across layers. We then orthogonalize each raw direction against the others to obtain 'pure' directions that isolate the unique effect of the target variable, free of confounding from co-varying factors. Using activation addition at inference time, we causally intervene on the residual stream and measure the change in the model's transfer decision in a dictator-game setting, both amplifying and attenuating the variable's baseline effect. Our analysis reveals selectivity: steering one direction shifts the intended variable's effect while leaving the effects of the other variables largely intact. We compare linearly extracted directions against concept-erasure baselines and probing controls, and evaluate portability across model sizes and instruction-tuned variants. Findings support the hypothesis that persona-conditioned decisions are mediated by locatable, editable directions rather than by surface lexical patterns alone.

sub_queries.semantic_query: large language models as proxies for human participants in dictator ultimatum public-goods economic games, persona-conditioned decisions, demographic prompting gender age effects on giving and fairness, instruction framing effects, alignment and debiasing of LLM social agents in simulation
sub_queries.hyde_text: We investigate the use of large language models as substitutes for human participants in canonical behavioral-economics experiments, focusing on the dictator game with a fixed endowment and a fair-split reference. We manipulate demographic personas (gender, age), instruction framings, and situational cues such as anticipated meeting with the receiver, and analyze how each variable shifts the LLM's chosen transfer amount. Our analysis compares the resulting effects to human meta-analytic findings and tests whether the LLM reproduces qualitative regularities such as gender-of-dictator and age-of-dictator effects on giving. We further examine whether such shifts arise as genuine internal responses to the social variable or as surface lexical patterns, and consider implications for alignment, debiasing, and the interpretability of LLM-based social simulations.
